newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-The misguided debate on EMU criteria -Juer.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-The misguided debate on EMU criteria -Juer.

text.p: By Juergen Pfister, Head of Economics Research, Commerzbank, Frankfurt

As the time draws nearer to decide on the launch of European monetary union and the participating countries, the question of whether Germany will meet the convergence criteria at all is becoming more significant.

Here the focus is exclusively on the two criteria relating to the public finances: the government's budget deficit and the level of government debt. In view of Germans' highly sceptical attitude towards monetary union, the federal government, and above all finance minister Waigel, have repeatedly stressed that Germany sets great store by the criteria being strictly met, especially that relating to the deficit: "three means three."

However, some people have pointed out that the Maastricht treaty does not require the fiscal criteria to be fulfilled so precisely down to the last decimal point. Rather, a "process" in the direction of the stated reference values is quite sufficient. This view not only fails to recognize the political and legal background to the "three means three" standpoint, but is also unhelpful given the set-up in Germany.

For one thing, the federal government's narrow interpretation of the budget-deficit criterion has to be seen in connection with the ruling of the Federal Constitutional Court on the Maastricht treaty and the resolution of the Bundestag, calling for "narrow and strict interpretation" of the convergence criteria.

Secondly, the federal government can only exert a decisive influence over the selection of participating countries in monetary union if it has a "clean record" itself. In other words, it has to be seen to fulfil unequivocally the budget-deficit criterion on which debate is focusing, proving that "three means three".
Thirdly and finally, most Germans either remain sceptical about monetary union or reject it altogether.
Put briefly, confidence is lacking that the promise can be kept that the euro will be as stable as the D-mark.

Against this background, it would be an important confidence-building achievement if the deficit criterion were met exactly on target. Conversely, it holds true that if things are not taken so seriously before monetary union is launched, this might also have an impact on the promised stability.

In addition to the legal and political restrictions, there is the fact that Germany gains nothing from the apparently elegant shift from a "strict application of the criteria" to a "strict application of the treaty".

The Maastricht treaty does indeed contain the familiar exemption clauses as regards the reference value tor the public-sector deficit: Either the deficit has declined substantially and continuously and has reached a level that comes close to the reference value or the excess over the reference value is only exceptional and temporary (Art. lO4c, EU Treaty).

A glance at Germany's figures will immediately reveal that its deficit ratio can neither be claimed to be declining towards 3%, nor has the deficit exceeded 3% only "temporarily and exceptionally". The deficit has overshot no less than five times in the seven years since 1991.

The situation is even more serious as regards government debt. This criterion may be regarded as economically less significant or the reference value can be considered arbitrarily selected. As far as the treaty is concerned, however, this is immaterial.

Above all: there is certainly no exemption clause for Germany's case of a rising trend for the debt to GDP ratio, away from the reference value. Anyone insisting on a "strict application of the treaty" in this context will relegate Germany to the sidelines in terms of monetary union.

One possible way of squaring political will with economic reason might take the form of the following solution. The treaty provides for the heads of state and government to decide on EMU membership taking into account the convergence reports of the European Monetary Institute and the European Commission. (As far as we can tell today, it is by no means likely that the two reports will reach identical conclusions.)

The more unimportant the reference values established by the convergence criteria become, the less a country will be able to demand access to monetary union solely by virtue of meeting these numbers. (This would naturally no longer hold true if all the criteria were unequivocally met. But it is a well-known fact that only Luxembourg will attain this goal.)
If, therefore, the political element is gaining greater influence in this way, it has to be utilised in order to secure the greatest possible likelihood of European monetary union becoming a success.

The central formula in this respect is offered by the treaty with its reference to the sustainability of convergence - a point which received political confirmation from the heads of state and government at last December's EU summit in Dublin.
As a result, the core monetary union - comprising Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and possibly Ireland and Finland - has a good chance of being realized in 1999.

Given the right political will to do so, Germany can undoubtedly meet the deficit criterion in 1997. The measures with a volume of DM10bn necessary for this purpose should primarily be realised on the spending side.
